{{Short description|American biologist}}
'''Paul Montgomery Bingham''' (born February 25, 1951) is an American [[molecular biologist]] and [[evolutionary biologist]], Associate Professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Cell Biology at [[Stony Brook University]]<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=Biochemistry faculty profile|url=http://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/biochem/research/faculty/bingham/|publisher=SUNY Stonybrook|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref> and Vice President for Research at Rafael Pharmaceuticals.<ref>{{cite web|title=Paul Bingham, Ph.D.Vice President of Research|url=https://rafaelpharma.com/leadership/executive-management|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210223051329/https://rafaelpharma.com/leadership/executive-management|archive-date=23 February 2021|access-date=23 February 2021|publisher=Rafael Pharmaceuticals}}</ref> He is known for his work in molecular biology, and has also published recent articles and a book on human evolution.<ref>{{cite web|title=Paul Bingham|url=https://www.worldsciencefestival.com/participants/paul-bingham/|access-date=2021-04-22|website=World Science Festival|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Biography==
Bingham received his undergraduate degree at [[Blackburn College (Illinois)|Blackburn College]] in [[Carlinville, Illinois]], and then completed his PhD in [[Biochemistry]] and [[Molecular biology|Molecular Biology]] at [[Harvard University]] in 1980 (thesis advisor, [[Matthew Meselson]]) after completing an MS in Microbiology at the University of Illinois (with [[John W. Drake]]).<ref name=":1">{{cite web|title=Paul Bingham {{!}} SUNY: Stony Brook University - Academia.edu|url=https://sbsuny.academia.edu/PaulBingham|access-date=2021-04-22|website=sbsuny.academia.edu}}</ref> He spent two years at the [[NIEHS|National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS)]] before joining the faculty of the Department of Biochemistry and [[Cell biology|Cell Biology]] and the School of Medicine at [[Stony Brook University]] in 1982.<ref name=":0" />

== Molecular biology ==
He was part of a collaborative team that discovered the [[parasitic]] [[DNA]] sequence element, the [[P element]] transposon.<ref>{{cite web|title=2012-13 ALLELE Series|url=http://evolution.ua.edu/2012-13-series.html|access-date=2021-04-22|website=ALLELE Seminar Series|language=en}}</ref> This enabled a widely used strategy still used today for retrieving genes from animals. It also shed fundamental new light on how [[evolution]] shapes the (self-interested) individual genes that collaborate to build [[organism]]s.

With his wife (Zuzana Zachar), he demonstrated that [[transposon]] insertion mutations were responsible for most of the [[alleles]] used in the development of [[classical genetics]].<ref name = "Zachar_1982">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zachar Z, Bingham PM | title = Regulation of white locus expression: the structure of mutant alleles at the white locus of Drosophila melanogaster | journal = Cell | volume = 30 | issue = 2 | pages = 529–41 | date = September 1982 | pmid = 6291773 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(82)90250-1 | s2cid = 25146339 }}</ref> He also collaborated with [[Carl Wu]] and [[Sarah Elgin]] (then at Harvard) on fundamental properties of metazoan [[chromatin]] structure.<ref name = "Wu_1979">{{cite journal | vauthors = Wu C, Bingham PM, Livak KJ, Holmgren R, Elgin SC | title = The chromatin structure of specific genes: I. Evidence for higher order domains of defined DNA sequence | journal = Cell | volume = 16 | issue = 4 | pages = 797–806 | date = April 1979 | pmid = 455449 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(79)90095-3 | s2cid = 10025372 }}</ref> In collaboration with Margaret Kidwell, then at Brown University, and Gerry Rubin, then at the Carnegie Institution, he carried out the [[molecular cloning]] of the P element transposon in [[Drosophila]].<ref name = "Bingham_1982">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bingham PM, Kidwell MG, Rubin GM | date = July 1982 | title = The molecular basis of P-M hybrid dysgenesis: the role of the P element, a P-strain-specific transposon family | journal = Cell | volume = 29 | issue = 3 | pages = 995–1004 | pmid = 6295641 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(82)90463-9 | s2cid = 18723067 }}</ref> This work revolutionized the retrieval of genes in Drosophila and subsequently contributed to progress in [[metazoan]] molecular and developmental genetics.<ref name = "Rabinow_1989">{{cite journal| vauthors = Rabinow L, Birchler JA |date=1989-03-01|title=A dosage-sensitive modifier of retrotransposon-induced alleles of the Drosophila white locus. |journal=The EMBO Journal|language=en|volume=8|issue=3|pages=879–889|doi=10.1002/j.1460-2075.1989.tb03449.x|pmid=2542025|pmc=400888|issn=1460-2075|doi-access=free}}</ref> He and his collaborators were the first to propose the use of P element [[transposon tagging]] to clone the first metazoan [[RNA]] polymerase subunit.<ref name = "Searles_1982">{{cite journal | vauthors = Searles LL, Jokerst RS, Bingham PM, Voelker RA, Greenleaf AL | date = December 1982 | title = Molecular cloning of sequences from a Drosophila RNA polymerase II locus by P element transposon tagging | journal = Cell | volume = 31 | issue = 3 Pt 2 | pages = 585–92 | pmid = 6297774 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(82)90314-2 | s2cid = 1985358 }}</ref> This work demonstrated that the P element is a recently invading parasite of the Drosophila genome and gene pool. Thus, P became the first clearly defined metazoan example of this long-suspected phenomenon.<ref name = "Rabinow_1989" />

His research group also worked on the nature of metazoan gene regulation<ref name = "Zachar_1989">{{cite book | vauthors = Zachar Z, Bingham PM | date = 1989 | doi = 10.1016/S0079-6603(08)60163-4 | title = Suppressible Insertion-Induced Mutations in Drosophila | volume = 36 | pages = 87–98 | pmid = 2544017 | series = Progress in Nucleic Acid Research and Molecular Biology | isbn = 978-0-12-540036-7 }}</ref> and the elucidation of the first case of autoregulation of gene expression at the level of [[pre-mRNA]] splicing<ref name = "Chou_1987">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chou TB, Zachar Z, Bingham PM | title = Developmental expression of a regulatory gene is programmed at the level of splicing | journal = The EMBO Journal | volume = 6 | issue = 13 | pages = 4095–104 | date = December 1987 | pmid = 2832151 | pmc = 553892 | doi = 10.1002/j.1460-2075.1987.tb02755.x }}</ref><ref name = "Zachar_1987" >{{cite journal | vauthors = Zachar Z, Chou TB, Bingham PM | title = Evidence that a regulatory gene autoregulates splicing of its transcript | journal = The EMBO Journal | volume = 6 | issue = 13 | pages = 4105–11 | date = December 1987 | pmid = 3443103 | pmc = 553893 | doi = 10.1002/j.1460-2075.1987.tb02756.x }}</ref><ref name = "Bingham_1988">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bingham PM, Chou TB, Mims I, Zachar Z | date = May 1988 | title = On/off regulation of gene expression at the level of splicing | journal = Trends in Genetics | volume = 4 | issue = 5 | pages = 134–8 | pmid = 2853467 | doi = 10.1016/0168-9525(88)90136-9 }}</ref><ref name = "Spikes_1994">{{cite journal | vauthors = Spikes DA, Kramer J, Bingham PM, Van Doren K | title = SWAP pre-mRNA splicing regulators are a novel, ancient protein family sharing a highly conserved sequence motif with the prp21 family of constitutive splicing proteins | journal = Nucleic Acids Research | volume = 22 | issue = 21 | pages = 4510–9 | date = October 1994 | pmid = 7971282 | pmc = 308487 | doi = 10.1093/nar/22.21.4510 }}
</ref> and of critical features of the nuclear organization of pre-mRNA processing and transport<ref name = "Li_1991">{{cite journal | vauthors = Li H, Bingham PM | title = Arginine/serine-rich domains of the su(wa) and tra RNA processing regulators target proteins to a subnuclear compartment implicated in splicing | journal = Cell | volume = 67 | issue = 2 | pages = 335–42 | date = October 1991 | pmid = 1655279 | doi = 10.1016/0092-8674(91)90185-2 | s2cid = 20307555 }}</ref><ref name = "Zachar_1993">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zachar Z, Kramer J, Mims IP, Bingham PM | date = May 1993 | title = Evidence for channeled diffusion of pre-mRNAs during nuclear RNA transport in metazoans | journal = The Journal of Cell Biology | volume = 121 | issue = 4 | pages = 729–42 | pmid = 8491768 | pmc = 2119787 | doi = 10.1083/jcb.121.4.729 }}</ref> This latter work first clearly established the now-widely accepted model of channeled diffusion for the movement of most pre-mRNAs through the nuclear compartment.<ref name=":1" /><ref name = "Kramer_1994">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kramer J, Zachar Z, Bingham PM | date = February 1994 | title = Nuclear pre-mRNA metabolism: channels and tracks | journal = Trends in Cell Biology | volume = 4 | issue = 2 | pages = 35–7 | pmid = 14731863 | doi = 10.1016/0962-8924(94)90001-9 }}</ref>

Bingham and Zachar discovered the first-in-class anti-cancer mitochondrial metabolism drug (CPI-613; [[devimistat]]),<ref name=":2">{{cite web|title=Executive Management Team|url=https://rafaelpharma.com/leadership/executive-management|access-date=2021-04-22|website=Rafael Pharmaceuticals|language=en}}</ref> currently in Phase III registrational clinical trials in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and [[acute myeloid leukemia]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Rafael cornerstone starts phase III pancreatic trial; CPI-613 in AML study, too|url=https://www.bioworld.com/articles/393003-rafael-cornerstone-starts-phase-iii-pancreatic-trial-cpi-613-in-aml-study-too?v=preview|access-date=2021-04-22|website=www.bioworld.com|language=en}}</ref> This work is now being done in collaboration with Rafael Pharmaceuticals.<ref name=":2" />

==Human evolutionary biology==

In the mid-1990s, he developed a theory of human uniqueness that proposes a novel explanation of why humans have evolved to be ecologically dominant. The theory has been published in three peer-reviewed journals: ''[[The Quarterly Review of Biology]]'', ''[[Evolutionary Anthropology]]'' and the ''[[Journal of Theoretical Biology]]''.<ref name = "Okada_2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Okada D, Bingham PM | title = Human uniqueness-self-interest and social cooperation | journal = Journal of Theoretical Biology | volume = 253 | issue = 2 | pages = 261–70 | date = July 2008 | pmid = 18462758 | doi = 10.1016/j.jtbi.2008.02.041 | bibcode = 2008JThBi.253..261O }}</ref><ref name = "Bingham_1999">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bingham PM | date = 1999 | doi = 10.1086/393069 | title = Human uniqueness: A general theory | journal = Quarterly Review of Biology | volume = 74 | issue = 2| pages = 133–169 | s2cid = 59499229 }}</ref>

He and co-author Joanne Souza have developed the theory further in a self-published book, ''[[Death from a Distance and the Birth of a Humane Universe]]''.<ref name = "Bingham_2009">{{cite book    | vauthors = Bingham PM, Souza J | date = 2009 |title=Death from a Distance and the Birth of a Humane Universe |publisher= BookSurge |location= South Carolina, USA | isbn =978-1-4392-5412-7 }}</ref> This work builds on [[W.D. Hamilton]]'s theory of [[kin selection]] (Benefit x Relatedness > Cost) and posits that the genus ''Homo'' evolved when an ancestral organism developed the ability to effectively manage non-kin conflicts of interests by lowering the [[cost of coercion]] between non-kin individuals (Benefit > Cost of Coercion + Cost of Cooperation).<ref name="Bingham_2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bingham PM, Souza J | title = Theory testing in prehistoric North America: fruits of one of the world's great archeological natural laboratories | journal = Evolutionary Anthropology | volume = 22 | issue = 3 | pages = 145–53 | date = 2013 | pmid = 23776052 | doi = 10.1002/evan.21359 }}</ref>

The theory, using precedents established in biological theory, proposes to explain many aspects of human social and sexual behavior. It proposed to account for the [[evolution]] of the human species from the advent of its phylogenetic branching from other hominins through physiological and behavioral adaptations until our current civilization.<ref name="Bingham_1999b" /> This theory of [[human uniqueness]] claims to answer the fundamental scientific challenge posed by [[Charles Darwin]], to explain the descent of man: how did the 'incremental' process of evolution by natural selection suddenly produce an utterly unprecedented kind of animal, humans? It suggests an explanation of [[human evolution|human origins]], and also of human properties (from speech to political/economic/religious behavior).<ref name = "Sterelny_2012">{{cite book | vauthors = Sterelny K |title=The evolved apprentice: how evolution made humans unique |date=2012 |publisher=The MIT Press |location=Cambridge, Mass. |isbn=978-0-262-52666-1 |url=https://dokumen.pub/the-evolved-apprentice-how-evolution-made-humans-unique-9780262016797-2011020798-9780262302814-9780262526661.html}}</ref>

According to his theory, the cost to an enforcer of coercing a cheating individual into a cooperative effort, known as the [[free-rider problem]], was lowered when a precursor species to humans developed a way to threaten adult conspecifics from a distance by evolving the ability to throw projectiles with sufficient skill to reliably injure the cheater, especially conjointly with others.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Boyd R, Gintis H, Bowles S | title = Coordinated punishment of defectors sustains cooperation and can proliferate when rare | journal = Science | volume = 328 | issue = 5978 | pages = 617–20 | date = April 2010 | pmid = 20431013 | doi = 10.1126/science.1183665 | bibcode = 2010Sci...328..617B }}</ref> This reduced the personal risk to multiple enforcers as formulated by [[Lanchester's Square Law]], when they gang up on a cheater.
<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Johnson DD, MacKay NJ | title = Fight the power: Lanchester's laws of combat in human evolution. | journal = Evolution and Human Behavior | date = March 2015 | volume = 36 | issue = 2 | pages = 152–63 | doi = 10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2014.11.001 | bibcode = 2015EHumB..36..152J }}</ref>
The theory proposes that this elite throwing ability initially allowed bands of proto-humans improved capacity to repel predators and scavenge their kills in the African savanna.
It was later adapted as threat projection towards free-riding conspecifics (cheaters) in non-kin [[Co-operation (evolution)|cooperative]] groups
that made the cooperation evolutionarily stable against cheaters who, without coercion by this threat, would otherwise flourish and displace co-operators.<ref>{{cite web|last=niallmck1|title=Self-Interested or Super-Cooperators? Human Nature from an Evolutionary Perspective|url=https://theweekenduniversity.com/evolution-human-nature/|access-date=2021-04-22|website=The Weekend University|date=24 January 2021 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The theory further generalizes to a theory of history,<ref name="Bingham_2013" /> claiming to account for many salient events of the two-million-year course of the human lineage—from the evolution of the genus ''Homo'' to the inception of [[behavioral modernity]] to the [[Neolithic Revolution]]<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bingham PM, Souza J, Blitz JH | title = Introduction: social complexity and the bow in the prehistoric North American record | journal = Evolutionary Anthropology | volume = 22 | issue = 3 | pages = 81–8 | date = May 2013 | pmid = 23776043 | doi = 10.1002/evan.21353 }}</ref> to the rise of the [[nation-state]].<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Poe M, Bingham P, Souza J |date=2010-04-30|title=P. Bingham and J. Souza, "Death From a Distance and the Birth of a Humane Universe"|url=https://ir.uiowa.edu/history_nbih/105|journal=New Books Network}}</ref><ref name="Bingham_1999b">{{cite journal| vauthors = Bingham PM |date=1999-12-01|title=Becoming Human: Evolution and Human Uniqueness. Ian Tattersall |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology|volume=74|issue=4|pages=499|doi=10.1086/394207|issn=0033-5770}}</ref><ref name = "Bingham_2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bingham PM | date = 2000 | doi = 10.1002/1520-6505(2000)9:6<248::AID-EVAN1003>3.0.CO;2-X | title = Human evolution and human history: A complete theory | journal = Evolutionary Anthropology | volume = 9 | issue = 6| pages = 248–257 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Academic work ==

In collaboration with Joanne Souza, he has developed a course [http://moya.ic.sunysb.edu/Class/bio358/instructors.htm] on the logic and implications of this new theory [http://www.stonybrook.edu/ugadmissions/programs/Paul_Bingham.shtml].

Bingham has served as the Faculty Director of the Freshmen College of Human Development at Stony Brook [http://www.sunysb.edu/ucolleges/hdv/humanabout.shtml].

Bingham also serves on the management team of Rafael Pharmaceuticals, a firm developing cancer therapies, as Vice President of Research. He and his collaborator, Prof. Zuzana Zachar, recently received the Maffetone Research Prize from the Carol M. Baldwin Breast Cancer Research Fund for their cancer work.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=Biochemistry faculty profile|url=http://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/biochem/research/faculty/bingham/|publisher=SUNY Stonybrook|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref><ref name=":2" />
